blurb: weighted by domain · single and multiple-response · mixed order

questions.stem: A developer adds {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful travel assistant."} as the first item in the messages list and receives a 400 error. What is the correct fix?
options: Move the text to the top-level system parameter of the request
Place the system message last so that it takes priority
Send the system text in a custom HTTP request header
Rename the role to "developer" and send the request again
notes: System prompts are a top-level parameter. The messages list only accepts user and assistant roles.
Position does not matter; the role itself is not accepted.
Headers carry authentication and versioning, not prompt content.
There is no developer role in the Messages API.

questions.stem: Which set of fields is required in every Messages API request?
options: model, max_tokens and messages
model, system and messages
model, messages and temperature
model, max_tokens and stream
notes: These three are mandatory. Everything else, including system and temperature, is optional.
system is optional, and max_tokens is missing.
temperature is optional, and max_tokens is missing.
stream is optional, and messages is missing.

questions.stem: A chatbot answers the first question well, but when the user follows up with "and what about the second one?", Claude has no idea what "the second one" refers to. The code sends only the newest user message on each call. What is the cause?
options: The API is stateless, so earlier turns must be resent
The session expired because the two calls were too far apart
The temperature is too low for the model to recall context
The model's context window was exceeded by the first answer
notes: Nothing is remembered between calls. The full history must be included in messages each time.
There is no server-side session to expire.
Temperature affects sampling, not memory.
A short exchange is nowhere near the window; the history was simply not sent.

questions.stem:
This line works in testing but raises an exception in production after tools are added to the request:

    answer = response.content[0].text

What is the most likely reason?
options: Tool-enabled responses place the text in response.completion
The first block is sometimes tool_use, without text
The response body is returned as a string once tools are enabled
The SDK needs an additional await when tools are present
notes: There is no completion field in the Messages API response.
content is a list of typed blocks. Code must check each block's type rather than assume the first is text.
The response shape is unchanged; content remains a list of blocks.
Whether a call is awaited depends on the client type, not on tools.

questions.stem: A report generator asks for a long JSON document. About one request in twenty fails with a JSON parse error near the end of the text. The HTTP status is always 200. What should the developer check first?
options: Whether the temperature is too high for producing JSON
Whether stop_reason is max_tokens, meaning the output was cut off
Whether the system prompt is longer than the user prompt
Whether the API key is being rate limited on some requests
notes: Temperature may vary wording but would not cut the document off at the end.
A 200 only means the request was processed. Truncation is reported through stop_reason, and truncated JSON cannot parse.
Relative prompt lengths have no bearing on truncated output.
Rate limiting returns 429, not a 200 with partial content.

questions.stem: A response arrives with stop_reason "tool_use". What must the application do next?
options: Show the response text to the user as the final answer
Run the tool and send a tool_result in a user turn
Repeat the same request until stop_reason is end_turn
Increase max_tokens, because the response was truncated
notes: The turn is not finished; Claude is waiting for a tool result.
tool_use means Claude is waiting for your code to execute the tool and return the result.
Repeating the request without a tool result just produces the same tool call.
Truncation is reported as max_tokens, not tool_use.

questions.stem: An application uses a server-side web search tool. A response comes back with stop_reason "pause_turn". What is the correct handling?
options: Treat it as a refusal and show an apology to the user
Execute the search in your own code and return a tool_result
Send the assistant content back so Claude can continue
Discard the response and start a new conversation
notes: A pause is not a refusal; the work is simply unfinished.
Server tools run on the platform; there is no client tool call waiting.
pause_turn means a server-side tool loop paused. Returning the content unchanged lets it resume.
That throws away progress; the turn can be continued.

questions.stem: A request sets stop_sequences to ["###"]. The response has stop_reason "stop_sequence". Which statement is correct?
options: Claude declined to answer and used "###" as a marker
The output was truncated by the max_tokens limit
Claude produced "###", and so generation stopped there
The request failed validation because "###" is a reserved token
notes: Declining is reported as refusal.
That would be reported as max_tokens.
Custom stop sequences end generation, and the response reports the matched sequence.
It is a normal, successful response.

questions.stem: A team streams responses so users see text immediately. A new developer claims this also halves the total generation time. What is accurate?
options: Streaming halves total time because tokens are sent in parallel
Streaming is slower overall and should be avoided for chat
Streaming speeds the first token, not the total time
Streaming reduces cost because fewer tokens are billed
notes: Tokens are generated in sequence either way.
The overhead is negligible and perceived latency is far better.
Streaming changes when the user sees output, not how long generation takes.
Billing is identical for streamed and non-streamed responses.

questions.stem: While streaming, in which event does the final stop_reason arrive?
options: message_delta
message_start
content_block_stop
ping
notes: message_delta carries top-level changes such as stop_reason and final usage, just before message_stop.
message_start opens the message; stop_reason is not known yet.
That closes a single content block, not the message.
ping events are keep-alives with no message data.

questions.stem: During a streamed response, a tool call's arguments arrive as several input_json_delta events. How should the application obtain the tool input?
options: Wait for a tool_result event that contains the full input
Concatenate the partial_json strings and parse once at content_block_stop
Ignore the deltas and read the input from message_start
Parse each partial_json fragment as it arrives and merge the objects
notes: tool_result is something your application sends, not something it receives.
Each delta is a fragment of JSON. Only the accumulated string is valid JSON.
message_start arrives before any tool input is generated.
Individual fragments are not valid JSON on their own.

questions.stem: A streaming request returns HTTP 200 and begins sending text. Thirty seconds later the stream ends with an error event. What does this show?
options: The content already received is corrupted and must be discarded silently
The request was invalid and should have been rejected with a 400
Errors can occur mid-stream, so the client must cope
The SDK has a bug, because a 200 response cannot contain an error
notes: The partial content is not corrupt; the application decides whether to retry or show it.
An invalid request is rejected before the stream starts.
The status line is sent before generation finishes. Failures after that arrive as an error event in the stream.
This is documented behaviour for streaming.

questions.stem: A service receives 400 invalid_request_error on some requests. A teammate proposes wrapping the call in a loop that retries up to five times. What is the best response?
options: Agree, but add exponential backoff between the attempts
Agree, but switch to a larger model on the last attempt
Retry once only, because the second attempt usually succeeds
Don't retry: the request is malformed, so fix it
notes: Backoff helps with overload, not with an invalid request.
The error is about the request format, not model capability.
Nothing changes between attempts, so it will not succeed.
Client errors of this type are deterministic. The same request will fail the same way.

questions.stem: During a traffic spike an application receives 429 rate_limit_error. What should it do first?
options: Report an error to users, because 429 cannot be retried
Create a new API key so that the limit is reset
Retry immediately in a tight loop until a request succeeds
Wait for the time given in the retry-after header, then retry
notes: 429 is one of the retryable errors.
Limits apply to the organisation, not to a single key.
That makes the overload worse and prolongs the limit.
A 429 includes a retry-after header that says how long to wait.

questions.stem: What does a 529 overloaded_error indicate, and how should code respond?
options: The model ID does not exist; correct it before trying again
The API key is invalid; replace it before trying again
The request body is too large; shrink it before trying again
The API is temporarily overloaded; retry with exponential backoff
notes: That is 404 not_found_error.
That is 401 authentication_error.
That is 413 request_too_large.
529 is a transient server-side condition and is safe to retry after a delay.

questions.stem: A newly deployed service gets 401 authentication_error on every call, while the same code works on the developer's laptop. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model is overloaded in the deployment's region
The deployed service is sending requests too quickly
The prompt contains content that the model refuses
The API key is missing or wrong in that environment
notes: That would produce 529.
That would produce 429.
A refusal is a 200 response with a stop_reason, not a 401.
401 means the key was not supplied or is not valid. Environment differences are the usual reason.

questions.stem: A client uploads a very large PDF inline and the API returns 413. Which action addresses the cause?
options: Reduce the request size, for example by splitting the document
Switch to streaming so that the upload is sent in chunks
Raise max_tokens so that the model can read the whole file
Retry with exponential backoff until the request is accepted
notes: 413 request_too_large means the body exceeds the size limit. Only a smaller request helps.
Streaming affects the response, not the size of the request.
max_tokens limits output; it does not affect request size.
The request will be too large every time.

questions.stem: A developer wraps every SDK call in a custom loop that retries five times on failure. During an outage, each user action produces far more API calls than expected. Why?
options: The SDK retries by default, so layers multiply
The API duplicates every request during an outage
The SDK opens one connection per token it generates
Each retry is billed as a batch of one hundred requests
notes: The official SDKs retry transient errors twice by default. An outer loop multiplies that.
The API does not duplicate requests.
Connections are not opened per token.
Retries are ordinary single requests.

questions.stem: A non-streaming request that generates a very long document fails intermittently with timeouts and dropped connections. What is the recommended change?
options: Use streaming, so that data flows continuously during generation
Lower max_tokens to 256 so that responses return quickly
Send the request twice in parallel and keep the faster one
Set max_retries to zero so that the failure surfaces sooner
notes: Long idle connections are fragile. Streaming keeps the connection active and is recommended for long outputs.
That would truncate the document the task needs.
That doubles cost and still risks both timing out.
That removes recovery without fixing the cause.

questions.stem: A customer reports a strange answer from yesterday. Which logged value is most useful when asking Anthropic support to investigate that specific call?
options: The request ID returned in the response headers
The local timestamp of the user's click
The temperature value used for the request
The first eight characters of the API key
notes: Every response has a unique request-id that identifies the exact call.
Timestamps are imprecise and not unique.
A parameter value does not identify a request.
Key fragments identify the account, not a single request.

questions.stem: A dashboard shows average usage at 60% of the requests-per-minute limit, yet the application still receives occasional 429 errors at the top of each hour when a scheduled job starts. Why?
options: Scheduled jobs are counted twice against the limit
A token bucket lets a sudden burst exceed capacity
Rate limits are reset to zero at the start of each hour
429 is returned at random to keep usage below 50%
notes: Requests are counted once regardless of origin.
The limit is not a simple per-minute counter. Short bursts can drain the bucket even when the average is low.
There is no hourly reset that lowers capacity.
Limits are deterministic, not random.

questions.stem: An application with a large, repeated system prompt keeps hitting its input-tokens-per-minute limit. Which change raises effective throughput without asking for higher limits?
options: Raise the temperature, since it reduces the tokens processed
Cache the prompt, since cached reads are mostly exempt
Lower max_tokens, since it is counted against the input limit
Enable streaming, since streamed tokens are not rate limited
notes: Temperature does not change token counts.
On most current models cache_read_input_tokens are excluded from ITPM, so caching increases throughput.
max_tokens concerns output and is not counted against input limits.
Streaming does not change rate-limit accounting.

questions.stem: Before sending a request that includes a long document, a service wants to know whether it will fit and which model to route it to. What is the best approach?
options: Divide the character count by ten to estimate the tokens
Set max_tokens to zero to get a free dry run
Call the token counting endpoint before sending
Send the request and read usage from the error response
notes: A crude ratio is unreliable, especially with tools, images or non-English text.
max_tokens must be positive; this is not a dry-run mechanism.
count_tokens accepts the same system, messages and tools as a real request and returns the input token count at no charge.
That wastes a call and may fail or cost money.

questions.stem: Which statement about the token counting endpoint is correct?
options: It is billed at the input rate and shares the Messages rate limit
It returns both the input tokens and the predicted output tokens
It only supports plain text and rejects tools or images
It is free, separately limited, and gives an estimate
notes: It is free and separately limited.
Output length is not known before generation.
It accepts the same structured inputs as a message request.
Counting does not generate output, is not billed, and is limited separately from message creation.

questions.stem: A team submits 5,000 requests in one message batch and reads the results file line by line, assuming line N answers request N. Some answers end up attached to the wrong records. What is the fix?
options: Sort the results by their completion timestamp
Match each result to its request using custom_id
Add a sequence number to each prompt and ask Claude to repeat it
Submit the requests in smaller batches of exactly 100
notes: Completion time does not reflect submission order.
Batch results are not guaranteed to be in submission order. custom_id exists for matching.
Fragile and unnecessary when custom_id is provided.
Batch size does not make the order reliable.

questions.stem: Every night a company summarises 60,000 product reviews. Results are needed by the next morning. Which approach is most cost-effective?
options: Synchronous calls using the most capable model available
The Message Batches API, since nobody is waiting on each result
One request containing all 60,000 reviews in a single prompt
Synchronous calls with streaming enabled for every review
notes: That maximises cost with no stated quality need.
Batches are asynchronous and half the price, which suits large offline jobs.
It would exceed limits and give poor per-review results.
Streaming helps a waiting user, not an overnight job.

questions.stem: To cut costs, a product manager suggests sending live customer chat messages through the Message Batches API. What is the main problem?
options: Batches can only be submitted once per day
Batches do not support system prompts or tools
Batches are asynchronous and may take hours to finish
Batches cost more per token than synchronous calls
notes: There is no such restriction.
Batch requests accept normal Messages parameters.
A batch has no latency guarantee beyond finishing within its processing window.
They cost less, about half.

questions.stem: Which TWO errors are appropriate to retry automatically with backoff? (Select TWO.)
options: 400 invalid_request_error
401 authentication_error
429 rate_limit_error
529 overloaded_error
404 not_found_error
notes: The request is malformed and will fail again.
The key is wrong; retrying cannot fix it.
Rate limiting is temporary; wait and retry.
Overload is temporary; back off and retry.
The resource or model does not exist; retrying cannot fix it.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about the Messages API are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The system prompt is supplied as a top-level parameter
The application must resend prior turns to continue a conversation
A 200 status guarantees that the answer is complete
max_tokens sets the minimum length of the response
The API stores each conversation for 24 hours by default
notes: system is not a role inside messages.
The API is stateless.
stop_reason may still indicate truncation.
It is an upper limit on output.
No conversation state is kept between calls.

questions.stem: A developer sets max_tokens to 4,000 hoping for longer, more detailed answers, but replies remain short. Why?
options: The value is ignored unless streaming is enabled
Values above 1,024 are silently reduced by the API
max_tokens is a cap; ask for length in the prompt
max_tokens applies to the input rather than the output
notes: It applies to streamed and non-streamed responses alike.
Models support much larger outputs.
The parameter caps output. It does not instruct the model to write more.
It limits output tokens.

questions.stem: In an agent loop, a developer appends only the text of each assistant response to the history and discards the other blocks. The next request fails with an error about a tool_result. Why?
options: The history exceeded the limit of ten messages per request
Text blocks must be removed from history before tool results
The matching tool_use block is missing from the history
tool_result blocks are only valid in the system parameter
notes: There is no such ten-message limit.
Text blocks are allowed alongside tool_use blocks.
A tool_result must follow an assistant message that contains the matching tool_use block.
They belong in a user message.

questions.stem: A pipeline always performs the same three steps: translate a document, summarise it, then format the summary as HTML. A teammate proposes an autonomous agent with tools for each step. What is the better design?
options: A multi-agent system with one agent for each of the steps
One very long prompt that asks for all three results at once
A single agent with a higher turn limit to explore options
A prompt chain run by application code, with a check between steps
notes: Extra coordination cost with no benefit for a fixed sequence.
Harder to validate and debug than separate steps.
Autonomy adds unpredictability where none is needed.
When steps are fixed and known, a workflow is cheaper, faster and more predictable than an agent.

questions.stem: A help desk receives billing questions, technical faults and sales enquiries. Each type needs different instructions and tools. Which pattern fits best?
options: Evaluator-optimiser: draft a reply, then critique and revise it
A single general prompt that lists every rule for all types
Parallelisation: send each message to all three handlers
Routing: classify each message, then send it to a specialised prompt
notes: That improves one output; it does not pick a path.
Rules for different types interfere with one another.
Wasteful, and the answers then need reconciling.
Routing separates concerns, so each path can be tuned without harming the others.

questions.stem: An internal assistant must answer questions using the company's 4,000-page policy library, which changes monthly. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Rely on the model's training data to know the policies
Raise the temperature so that the model recalls more detail
Paste the full library into the system prompt on every request
Retrieve relevant passages and add them to the prompt
notes: The model has never seen private, changing documents.
Temperature does not add knowledge.
Likely too large, slow and costly.
Retrieval supplies current, relevant content without sending everything every time.

questions.stem: A web chat application needs multi-turn conversations. Where should conversation history be kept?
options: In a server-side store keyed by the application's own session ID
Nowhere, since the model retains recent conversations
In the system prompt, appended to after every turn
In the Claude API, retrieved with the previous message ID
notes: The application owns state. A backend store lets it reload and resend history securely.
The model retains nothing between calls.
History belongs in messages; rewriting the system prompt also defeats caching.
The API does not store conversations for retrieval.

questions.stem: Two browser tabs for the same user send messages to the same conversation at almost the same moment. Afterwards the stored history has turns out of order and one reply is missing. What should be added?
options: Per-session locking when the history is updated
A lower temperature so that both replies are identical
A second API key so that the two tabs do not collide
A longer max_tokens so that neither reply is dropped
notes: It is an ordinary concurrent-write problem on shared state, solved with ordinary concurrency control.
Sampling settings cannot fix a race condition.
Keys are unrelated to writes to your own store.
The reply was lost in storage, not truncated.

questions.stem: A mobile team wants the app to call the Claude API directly to avoid an extra network hop. What is the main objection?
options: The API key would ship in the app and be extractable
Direct calls are billed at a higher rate per token
The Claude API refuses requests from mobile devices
Mobile networks cannot carry server-sent events
notes: Client-side keys cannot be kept secret. Calls should go through a backend that holds the key.
Pricing does not depend on where the call originates.
The API does not identify device types.
They can; this is not the issue.

questions.stem: An extraction schema marks delivery_date as a required string. For emails that contain no date, the model returns a plausible but invented date. What is the best schema change?
options: Make the field nullable, returning null when absent
Mark the field required in two places for emphasis
Add a regular expression that enforces a date format
Lower the temperature so that the date is deterministic
notes: A required field with no source value pushes the model to invent one.
Emphasis does not create missing information.
The format was fine; the value was fabricated.
A deterministic invented date is still invented.

questions.stem: A ticket classifier uses an enum of five categories. Unusual tickets are being forced into badly fitting categories. Which change helps most?
options: Remove the enum and accept any free-text category
Add an "other" value, with a short free-text field for the detail
Add twenty more categories to cover every case
Send each ticket three times and take the majority label
notes: That loses the consistency the enum provides.
An escape value stops the model from being forced into a wrong label.
Large enums are harder to choose from and never cover everything.
Voting between wrong labels does not produce a right one.

questions.stem: An invoice extractor uses structured outputs, so every response matches the schema. Finance finds invoices where the line items do not add up to the stated total. What is missing?
options: A stricter schema with additionalProperties set to false
A semantic check in code that lines sum to the total
A higher max_tokens value so that totals are not truncated
A system prompt reminder that totals must be accurate
notes: The structure was already valid; the values were wrong.
A schema guarantees structure, not correctness. Business rules need their own validation.
Nothing was truncated.
A reminder is not verification.

questions.stem: After a timeout, a workflow retried a step, and a customer was refunded twice. Which design principle prevents this?
options: Increase the timeout to ten minutes for every call
Make the side effect idempotent, using an idempotency key
Ask the model to remember which refunds it has issued
Disable all retries across the whole application
notes: Timeouts can still occur; duplicates remain possible.
With an idempotency key, a repeated attempt is recognised and not executed again.
Model memory is not a reliable transaction record.
That sacrifices resilience; the issue is the repeated side effect.

questions.stem: The Claude API has been returning errors for several minutes. Every user request waits through multiple retries and then fails. What should the application do instead?
options: Return an empty reply so that users don't see any error
Stop calling after repeated failures and fall back
Remove the timeout so that requests can wait as long as needed
Increase the retry count so that requests eventually pass
notes: Silent empty answers hide the failure and confuse users.
A circuit breaker with graceful degradation avoids piling up slow, doomed requests.
Hanging requests exhaust resources and frustrate users.
More retries deepen the pile-up during an outage.

questions.stem: A marketing campaign sends bursts of thousands of requests within a few seconds, causing many 429 errors, although total daily volume is well within limits. Which design smooths this out?
options: Raise max_tokens so that each request does more work
Open more connections so that the burst finishes sooner
Put requests on a queue and process them at a controlled rate
Disable SDK retries so that failures return faster
notes: It does not reduce the request rate.
That intensifies the burst.
A queue absorbs bursts and feeds the API at a steady pace.
Requests would simply fail instead of completing.

questions.stem: A model ID is hard-coded in forty source files. A newer model must now be adopted. Which practice would have made this a small change?
options: Letting each developer choose the model on their machine
Storing the model ID inside the system prompt text
Keeping the model ID in configuration, read by all the call sites
Using a different model ID in every file for flexibility
notes: Uncontrolled variation between environments.
The prompt does not select the model.
Configuration lets the model change without editing code across the codebase.
That makes the system even harder to manage.

questions.stem: Production behaviour changed slightly overnight with no deployment. The service uses a model alias that always points to the newest version. What is the recommended practice?
options: Keep the alias and add more few-shot examples each week
Keep the alias and lower the temperature to stabilise output
Pin a specific model version and upgrade deliberately after testing
Switch aliases every day to average out the differences
notes: Examples do not prevent the underlying model from changing.
Sampling settings do not prevent a model change.
A moving alias can change behaviour without warning. Pinning makes upgrades a tested release.
That adds variation rather than removing it.

questions.stem: A developer edits one paragraph of a production system prompt and deploys it directly. The next day, a previously working feature is broken. Which process was missing?
options: A longer system prompt with more capital letters
A rule that only senior developers may edit prompts
A higher max_tokens setting in production
Versioned prompts and evals before release
notes: Emphasis is not a release process.
Seniority does not replace testing.
Unrelated to the regression.
A prompt change is a behaviour change. Regression evals catch breakage before users do.

questions.stem: After launch, which set of measurements best shows the health of a Claude-powered feature?
options: Error rates, latency, token cost, validation failures
The average temperature across all the requests
The count of developers who can access the API key
The number of lines in the system prompt each week
notes: Together these cover reliability, speed, spend and output quality.
A configuration value, not an outcome.
An access-control fact, not a health metric.
Prompt length says nothing about behaviour in production.

questions.stem: In a multi-tenant application, a user of one company receives an answer that quotes another company's document. Where is the flaw?
options: The temperature allowed the model to be creative
The system prompt did not forbid sharing documents
Retrieval was not scoped to the authenticated user's tenant
The model's context window was too large
notes: The other tenant's content was in the context; this is not creativity.
A prompt rule cannot undo data that was already supplied.
Isolation must be enforced when data is fetched, before anything reaches the prompt.
Window size does not select which documents are retrieved.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices are appropriate for managing configuration of a Claude application? (Select TWO.)
options: Embed prompts as string literals spread across the modules
Load the API key from a secret manager or environment variable
Use separate keys and settings for development and production
Commit the API key in a private repository for convenience
Share one key across all teams to simplify rotation
notes: Scattered prompts are hard to version, review and test.
Keeps the key out of code and repositories.
Limits blast radius and separates usage.
Private repositories still leak; keys do not belong in source control.
A shared key widens exposure and hides who used what.

questions.stem: A team is deciding between synchronous calls and the Message Batches API for a new workload. Which TWO facts are most relevant to the decision? (Select TWO.)
options: Whether the developers prefer Python or TypeScript
Whether the system prompt uses XML tags or Markdown
Whether the prompts are written in British or American English
Whether a user or blocking process is waiting on each result
Whether a delay of up to several hours is acceptable
notes: Both SDKs support both modes.
Prompt formatting does not affect the choice.
Spelling variety has no bearing on the choice.
Batches are asynchronous, so waiting users rule them out.
Batch completion time is not immediate.

questions.stem: A sponsor asks a developer to "add AI to the returns process". What should the developer do first?
options: Write a long system prompt covering every case
Build a multi-agent prototype to show the sponsor
Choose the most capable model that is available
Clarify the goal and write measurable requirements
notes: There is nothing agreed yet for the prompt to implement.
Building before the goal is clear risks solving the wrong problem.
Model choice depends on requirements that don't exist yet.
An ambiguous goal cannot be designed or tested. Requirements come before model or pattern choices.

questions.stem: Which of these is an infrastructure (non-functional) requirement?
options: The system must draft a reply for an agent to approve
The system must extract the invoice number and total
The system must classify tickets into six categories
Responses must begin within two seconds at peak load
notes: That is a function the system performs.
That is a function the system performs.
That is a function the system performs.
It describes how well the system must perform, not what it does.

questions.stem: A requirement states: "Customer data must not leave the company's cloud region." Which design decision does this affect most directly?
options: Whether responses are parsed with Pydantic
Whether examples in the prompt use XML tags
Whether the temperature is set near 0 or 1
Which platform and deployment option is used
notes: Validation tooling is unrelated to data location.
Prompt formatting does not control where data is processed.
Sampling settings are unrelated to data location.
Data-residency constraints determine where and through which provider the model is called.

questions.stem: An application has run unchanged for a year. One morning every request fails with a 404 naming the model. Nothing was deployed. What life-cycle activity was neglected?
options: Maintenance: tracking model deprecations
Testing: the unit tests should have been stricter
Development: the code should have used raw HTTP
Design: the system should have used more agents
notes: Models are retired on a schedule. Operating an LLM system includes watching for that and migrating in time.
Unit tests cannot keep a retired model available.
The SDK is not the cause of a retired model.
Agent count has nothing to do with a retired model.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between an official Claude SDK and the REST API?
options: The SDK is a wrapper over the same REST API
The SDK is required; raw HTTP calls are rejected
The SDK uses a separate, faster private protocol
The SDK runs the model locally on your machine
notes: SDKs add typing, retries, timeouts and stream handling on top of the same HTTP endpoints.
Any HTTP client can call the API.
It calls the same public HTTP API.
Models run on the provider's servers.

questions.stem: A developer builds a JSON request body by joining strings and inserting the user's text directly. Requests fail whenever the text contains a quotation mark. What is the correct fix?
options: Wrap the user's text in a second pair of quotes
Serialise the object with a JSON library
Replace every quotation mark with a blank space
Ask users not to type quotation marks in the box
notes: Adds more unescaped quotes and makes the JSON worse.
A serialiser escapes special characters correctly. String concatenation does not.
Corrupts the user's text and misses other special characters.
Unreasonable, and other characters will also break it.

questions.stem: A script summarises 4,000 documents by launching all requests at once with asyncio.gather. Most fail with 429 errors. A user is waiting for the results. What is the best change?
options: Remove the awaits so that requests return sooner
Switch every call to the synchronous client instead
Limit concurrency with a semaphore or worker pool
Launch the same requests twice to improve the odds
notes: Without awaiting, results are never collected.
Sequential calls would be very slow for a waiting user.
Bounded concurrency keeps throughput high while staying inside rate limits.
Doubles the load that caused the errors.

questions.stem: A coding agent produced a change that passes the existing tests. What should happen before it is merged?
options: A person reviews the diff, edge cases included
The change is merged and reviewed after the release
Nothing further; passing tests are sufficient proof
The same session reviews and approves its own change
notes: Passing tests show only what the tests cover. Review is still needed for generated code.
Review after release finds problems too late.
Tests rarely cover every edge case or security concern.
A fresh reviewer avoids the author's blind spots.

questions.stem: A team wants an agent to migrate 180 files from one logging library to another. Which approach is most likely to succeed?
options: Let several agents edit the same files in parallel
Plan first, then migrate in small verified steps
Ask for all 180 files to be rewritten in one prompt
Skip the tests until every file has been converted
notes: Conflicting edits on shared files cause breakage.
Large refactors need a plan, a safety net of tests, and incremental verification.
Overloads context and gives no checkpoint when something breaks.
Errors compound and become hard to locate.

questions.stem: During code review, a reviewer notices that generated code imports a package nobody on the team has heard of. What is the right reaction?
options: Install it at once, since the model recommended it
Verify the package exists and is trustworthy
Assume it is a standard library the team forgot
Delete the import line and merge the remainder
notes: A recommendation is not verification.
Generated code can reference non-existent or unsuitable packages. Dependencies must be checked.
An assumption, not a check.
The code probably depends on it and would break.

questions.stem: Why does the Messages API use server-sent events for streaming, and not WebSockets?
options: WebSockets cannot carry text, only binary frames
Token streaming only needs one-way delivery
WebSockets are limited to a hundred messages
Server-sent events let the client send mid-stream
notes: WebSockets carry text as well as binary.
SSE provides one-way streaming over ordinary HTTP. WebSockets are for two-way communication.
There is no such limit.
SSE is one-way; the client does not send on it.

questions.stem: A browser-based voice assistant needs the client and the team's backend to exchange audio and control messages continuously in both directions. Which transport suits that link?
options: A series of separate GET requests
A nightly batch upload
Server-sent events alone
A WebSocket connection
notes: Polling is slow and one-directional per request.
A batch has no real-time interaction.
SSE only carries data from server to client.
WebSockets keep one connection open over which both sides can send at any time.

questions.stem: A prompt gives excellent results in the Claude chat app. Sent unchanged through the Messages API, results are noticeably different. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The API ignores the first message of each request
The API always serves an older and weaker model
The API adds no product system prompt, tools or memory
The API runs every request at temperature zero
notes: Every message sent is used.
The model is whichever one the request names.
Each surface assembles context differently. Through the API, Claude sees only what the request contains.
The default is not zero unless set.

questions.stem: In Claude Code, a team writes "Never run database migrations" in CLAUDE.md. A migration is later run during a session. Why was the instruction not a guarantee?
options: CLAUDE.md is limited to twenty lines of content
CLAUDE.md applies to Python files and no others
CLAUDE.md is guidance, not an enforced control
CLAUDE.md is only loaded on the first day of use
notes: There is no such limit.
It is not restricted by language.
Instructions are advisory. Enforcement needs a permission rule or a hook.
It is loaded in every session.

questions.stem: A developer has spent three hours in one Claude Code session on several unrelated tasks. Answers are getting worse and earlier instructions are being forgotten. What is the best practice?
options: Keep going and repeat each instruction in capitals
Paste the whole transcript back in as a reminder
Start a fresh session per task, carrying a short summary
Raise the max_tokens value for the next reply
notes: Adds more noise to an already crowded context.
Makes the context problem worse.
Unrelated history pollutes the context. Clean sessions with a deliberate hand-over work better.
Output size is not the issue.

questions.stem: A team wants every developer to have the same set of Claude Code skills, commands and hooks for a project. Which approach fits best?
options: Have each developer recreate them from memory
Email the files and ask each person to copy them
Describe them in the README without any files
Package them as a plugin enabled in the project settings
notes: Guarantees inconsistency.
Manual copies drift apart and are never updated together.
A description does not install anything.
A plugin bundles these components, and project settings share it with everyone who works in the repository.

questions.stem: Before installing a third-party Claude Code plugin, what is the most important consideration?
options: It should contain more commands than other plugins
It should be the newest plugin in the marketplace
Its name should be shorter than twelve characters
It can run code, so its source must be trusted
notes: Size is not a measure of trust or quality.
Newness says nothing about safety.
Name length is irrelevant.
Plugins can execute code and extend what the agent can do. Treat them like any other dependency.

questions.stem: Output quality dropped last Tuesday. The team cannot tell which prompt text was in use that day, because prompts are edited directly in a dashboard. What practice is missing?
options: A larger context window for the affected model
A second dashboard with a different colour scheme
A rule that prompts may be edited only on Fridays
Prompt versioning, logged on each request
notes: Window size does not record prompt history.
Cosmetic and unrelated.
Scheduling edits does not record what changed.
Versioned prompts plus logging make it possible to connect a behaviour change to a specific prompt.

questions.stem: In Claude Code, which file should hold a personal permission override that must not be shared with the team?
options: .claude/settings.local.json
CLAUDE.md in the project root
.mcp.json in the project root
.claude/settings.json
notes: The local settings file is for personal overrides and is not committed.
It holds instructions, not permission settings, and is shared.
It lists shared MCP servers.
That file is committed and shared with the team.

questions.stem: An application is moved from the direct Claude API to a cloud vendor's platform. A beta feature it depends on stops working. What should have been checked first?
options: Whether that feature is available on the chosen platform
Whether the cloud vendor uses a faster network
Whether the team's laptops were recently updated
Whether the prompts were translated to English
notes: Feature availability, model identifiers and authentication differ between platforms.
Network speed does not add a missing feature.
Client machines are unrelated.
Language is unrelated to feature availability.

questions.stem: Which TWO are infrastructure (non-functional) requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: The service must flag invoices with missing totals
The service must handle 50 requests per second at peak
The service must produce a summary for each ticket
Prompts and outputs must be retained for no more than 30 days
The service must translate documents into French
notes: A function.
A throughput constraint.
A function.
A data-retention constraint.
A function.

questions.stem: Which statement about tokens and pricing is correct?
options: Output tokens are priced higher than input tokens
Only output tokens are billed; input is free
Input and output tokens are always priced the same
Tokens are billed per request, whatever the length
notes: Output costs several times more per token, so trimming output is an effective saving.
Input tokens are billed too.
They are priced differently.
Billing is per token.

questions.stem: What does a model's context window limit?
options: The total input and output tokens in one request
How many days a conversation is stored by the API
The number of requests that can be sent per minute
The number of tools that may be defined in a request
notes: System prompt, tools, history and the generated output all share the window.
The API does not store conversations.
That is a rate limit.
Tools consume tokens but the window is measured in tokens.

questions.stem: A team moves to a model with a much larger context window and expects the assistant to remember users between sessions. It does not. Why?
options: Memory only works at temperature zero
A context window is per request and is not persistent memory
Large windows are only active when streaming is enabled
The window must first be enabled in the Console
notes: Temperature has nothing to do with persistence.
Whatever the size, the window holds only what is sent in that request.
Window size is unrelated to streaming.
It is a property of the model, not a setting.

questions.stem: A data-extraction task needs the most consistent output possible. Which setting is most appropriate?
options: A long list of stop sequences
A low temperature, close to 0
A high temperature, close to 1
A very small max_tokens value
notes: Stop sequences end output; they do not reduce variation.
Low temperature favours the most likely tokens and reduces variation.
That increases variety, the opposite of the goal.
That truncates output; it does not make it consistent.

questions.stem: A unit test sends a fixed prompt at temperature 0 and asserts that the reply equals a stored string. It passes most days and occasionally fails. What is the best fix?
options: Run the test five times and pass if any run matches
Assert on structure and key facts instead of exact text
Set top_p to 0 as well as temperature to force identity
Cache the first response and compare against it forever
notes: That hides flakiness instead of removing the fragile assertion.
Output is not guaranteed identical even at temperature 0. Tests should check properties.
No sampling setting guarantees identical output.
That tests the cache, not the model's behaviour.

questions.stem: A service must label two million short messages per day as spam or not spam, with low latency. Which starting point is most sensible?
options: Whichever tier leads a public coding leaderboard
The most capable tier, to be safe on every message
The smallest, fastest tier, verified against an eval set
The most capable tier, with extended thinking enabled
notes: A coding benchmark does not predict spam classification.
Far more cost and latency than a simple task needs.
Simple, high-volume classification suits the cheapest tier. Evals confirm whether it is good enough.
Thinking adds cost and delay to a task that needs neither.

questions.stem: A legal-analysis feature produces subtle reasoning errors on a mid-tier model. Volume is low and mistakes are costly. What should be tried?
options: The same tier with max_tokens reduced by half
A more capable tier, comparing results on the eval set
The same tier with a higher temperature setting
A smaller tier, because it will respond more quickly
notes: Shorter output does not fix reasoning errors.
With low volume and high error cost, capability outweighs price. Evals confirm the gain.
More randomness will not improve reasoning.
Speed is not the problem; reasoning quality is.

questions.stem: What is the most reliable basis for choosing between two model tiers for a specific product feature?
options: Selecting whichever model was released most recently
Selecting whichever model has the larger context window
Comparing both on your own eval set for the feature
Asking each model which of them is better at the task
notes: Newer does not mean better value for every task.
Window size is one factor and says little about quality on your task.
Only task-specific evaluation shows how each model performs on your workload.
Self-assessment is not evidence.

questions.stem: A support system handles simple FAQs and a small number of complex disputes. Which design best balances cost and quality?
options: Send everything to the largest model for consistency
Send everything to the smallest model to control cost
Route simple requests to a small model, hard ones up
Alternate between models on every request for fairness
notes: Overpays for the simple majority.
Under-serves the complex disputes.
Mixing tiers applies capability where it is needed and saves money elsewhere.
Random assignment ignores what each task needs.

questions.stem: Extended thinking is switched on for a feature that looks up a store's opening hours from a provided table. Cost and latency rise with no quality gain. Why?
options: Thinking forces the model to use the largest tier
Thinking doubles the size of the input prompt
Thinking disables prompt caching for the whole account
Thinking adds billed output and time a lookup doesn't need
notes: It does not change the model.
It adds output tokens, not input.
It does not disable caching account-wide.
Thinking helps complex multi-step reasoning. On simple tasks it only adds cost and delay.

questions.stem: A request includes a 9,000-token policy document marked with cache_control. The first response shows cache_creation_input_tokens of about 9,000 and cache_read_input_tokens of 0. What does this mean?
options: The cache is disabled for requests with a system prompt
Caching failed because no tokens were read from the cache
The document was too short to be eligible for caching
The prefix was cached now; later calls can read it
notes: System prompts are a typical thing to cache.
A first call always writes rather than reads.
Tokens were written, so it was eligible.
The first call pays the write. Subsequent matching calls within the lifetime show cache reads.

questions.stem: Caching is enabled on a long system prompt, but cache_read_input_tokens is always 0. The prompt begins with "Current date and time: " followed by a timestamp. What is the cause?
options: System prompts cannot be cached, only user messages
The cache lifetime is one second by default
The timestamp changes, so the prefix never matches
Caching only takes effect after 100 identical requests
notes: System prompts can be cached.
The default lifetime is five minutes.
A cache hit needs an identical prefix. Dynamic content must come after the cached section.
There is no such threshold.

questions.stem: How should a prompt be arranged to get the most from prompt caching?
options: Order is irrelevant, since caching matches by content hash
Changing content first, so that the model reads it sooner
Stable and changing content interleaved in small pieces
Stable content first, then whatever changes
notes: Matching is prefix-based; order matters.
A changing start invalidates the whole prefix.
The first change ends the reusable prefix.
Caching works on prefixes, so everything before the breakpoint must stay identical.

questions.stem: With default settings, how long does a cached prefix remain available?
options: Five minutes, refreshed each time it is read
Until the API key that wrote it is rotated
For exactly one further request, then it is deleted
Twenty-four hours from when it is first written
notes: The default lifetime is five minutes and each hit renews it. A one-hour option costs more to write.
Lifetime is time-based.
It can be read many times within its lifetime.
That is not the default lifetime.

questions.stem: How are cache writes and cache reads priced relative to normal input tokens (default five-minute cache)?
options: Writes cost about 1.25 times; reads about 0.1 times
Writes are free; reads cost the same as normal input
Writes and reads both cost half of normal input
Writes cost ten times more; reads are free
notes: There is a small premium to write and a large discount to read.
Writes carry a premium and reads are discounted.
That confuses caching with batch pricing.
Neither figure is right.

questions.stem: A tool that answers one-off questions, each with a completely different 300-token prompt, enables prompt caching. Costs do not fall. Why?
options: Nothing is repeated, and the prompts are too short
Caching only works with the Message Batches API
Caching needs temperature 0 to produce cache hits
Caching applies only to output tokens, not input
notes: Caching pays only when a sufficiently long prefix is reused.
It works with ordinary requests.
Sampling settings are not part of the match.
It applies to input prefixes.

questions.stem: A team reorders its tool definitions between requests, depending on which features are enabled. The cache hit rate collapses. Why?
options: Reordering tools raises the cache's minimum token size
Tools start the prefix, so changes invalidate the rest
Tool definitions are never included in cached content
Each tool definition needs its own cache breakpoint
notes: The minimum size does not depend on ordering.
The prefix order is tools, then system, then messages. A change early on breaks the rest.
They are part of the prefix.
One breakpoint after the tools is enough; only four exist.

questions.stem: A chatbot sends a 10,000-token system prompt, a short question and gets a short answer, thousands of times a day. Which single change is likely to cut cost the most?
options: Raising max_tokens on each request
Caching the system prompt
Lowering the temperature to zero
Enabling streaming on every response
notes: A higher cap cannot reduce cost.
The repeated prefix dominates input cost, and cache reads are charged at a fraction of the normal price.
Temperature does not change token counts.
Streaming does not change cost.

questions.stem: Which combination gives the lowest cost for a large overnight job where every request shares a long instruction block?
options: Synchronous calls together with extended thinking
Message Batches API together with prompt caching
Streaming together with a higher temperature
The largest model together with a higher max_tokens
notes: Thinking adds output cost and sync has no discount.
The batch discount and cache reads can be combined for work that is not time-sensitive.
Neither reduces cost.
Both tend to raise cost.

questions.stem: Responses are about 800 words and users complain about waiting. The content cannot be shortened. Which change most improves the experience at no extra cost?
options: Increase max_tokens to give the model more room
Use the Message Batches API for these requests
Stream the response so that text appears as it is generated
Add extended thinking so that the answer is planned
notes: A higher cap does not speed anything up.
Batches are asynchronous and far slower.
Streaming cuts perceived latency without changing the content or the price.
Thinking adds time before the answer starts.

questions.stem: Which factor usually has the largest effect on the total time of a single response?
options: Whether the system prompt uses XML tags
The alphabetical order of the tool names
The number of output tokens generated
The number of characters in the model ID
notes: Formatting has negligible effect.
Irrelevant.
Output is generated token by token, so longer answers take longer.
Irrelevant.

questions.stem: An agent occasionally runs for hundreds of turns and produces a large bill. Which control addresses this most directly?
options: A lower max_tokens value on each individual call
A longer system prompt asking the agent to be frugal
A total token or cost budget for the task
A higher temperature to encourage shorter runs
notes: Each call is smaller but the number of calls is unbounded.
A request, not a limit.
Per-call limits do not bound a loop. A task-level budget does.
Temperature does not bound the loop.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions would prevent a prompt-cache hit? (Select TWO.)
options: A different user question placed after the cache breakpoint
Sending the second request from a different server
A per-user greeting placed at the start of the cached block
More than the cache lifetime passing between requests
Using streaming for the second request but not the first
notes: Content after the breakpoint may vary freely.
The origin machine is not part of the match.
Any difference in the prefix breaks the match.
An expired entry cannot be read.
Streaming does not affect the match.

questions.stem: Which TWO changes reduce the actual end-to-end time of a response? (Select TWO.)
options: Raising the temperature
Using a smaller, faster model tier
Asking for a shorter answer
Logging the request ID
Raising the max_tokens limit
notes: Sampling randomness does not change speed.
Smaller tiers generate faster.
Fewer output tokens take less time.
Logging has no effect on generation time.
A higher cap does not speed generation.

questions.stem: An interactive coding tool uses a top-tier model and needs faster output without changing the model's quality. Cost is a secondary concern. Which option addresses this directly?
options: The Batches API, which returns results in seconds
A higher max_tokens, which makes generation faster
A smaller tier, which keeps the quality identical
Fast mode, which speeds up the same model at a premium
notes: Batches are asynchronous and slower.
The cap does not change speed.
A smaller model is faster but not the same quality.
Fast mode raises output speed for the same model at a higher price.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates model choice from reasoning mode?
options: Choosing a larger tier turns thinking on by default always
Enabling thinking switches the request to a larger tier
Thinking is only available on the smallest model tier
Picking a tier and enabling thinking are separate decisions
notes: Tier and thinking are configured separately.
The model stays the same.
It is not limited to the smallest tier.
A tier sets capability and price; thinking or effort settings control how much reasoning is done on a request.

questions.stem: A classification prompt works well zero-shot. A developer adds twelve long examples "to be safe". What is the main cost?
options: The context window is permanently reduced in size
The model is no longer able to return any labels
The API rejects prompts that contain examples
More input tokens on every request, with little benefit
notes: The window is per request, not permanently changed.
Examples do not prevent output.
Examples are allowed.
Examples are sent each time. When zero-shot already works, they add cost and latency for no gain.

questions.stem: A team upgrades to a newer model version. Token counts for the same prompts change, and some replies are formatted differently. What does this show?
options: The API key was rotated during the upgrade process
The prompts were corrupted while being transferred
The temperature setting is reset by every upgrade
Releases change behaviour; upgrades need evals
notes: Key rotation does not change model behaviour.
Nothing indicates corruption.
Request parameters are whatever the code sends.
New versions are not drop-in replacements. Pin versions, re-run evals and re-count tokens.

questions.stem: A prompt has tool definitions, a system prompt, a large reference document, and a growing conversation. Why might a developer set several cache breakpoints?
options: So parts that change at different rates cache apart
So that each breakpoint doubles the context window
So that output tokens are billed at the cache rate
So that the model reads the document several times
notes: A change only invalidates what follows it. Layered breakpoints keep stable sections cached.
They do not change the window.
Caching applies to input.
Breakpoints do not repeat content.

questions.stem: A company wants to know which product feature drives its Claude spend. What is the most direct approach?
options: Record the usage from each response, tagged by feature
Ask each team for an informal monthly impression
Estimate from the number of lines in each prompt
Compare the temperature used by each feature
notes: Each response reports input, output and cache tokens. Tagging them shows where cost goes.
Impressions are not measurements.
Line counts are a poor proxy for tokens.
Temperature does not indicate cost.

questions.stem: What is the defining difference between a workflow and an agent?
options: Code fixes a workflow's steps; an agent's model chooses
A workflow uses one model; an agent always uses several
A workflow runs in batch; an agent always runs in real time
A workflow cannot call tools; an agent always calls tools
notes: The distinction is who controls the sequence of actions.
Either can use one or many models.
Timing mode is unrelated.
Workflows can use tools too.

questions.stem: In a hand-written agent loop, what should decide whether to make another call to Claude?
options: Whether exactly ten iterations have been completed
Whether the response's stop_reason is tool_use
Whether the response is shorter than the previous one
Whether the response text contains the word "done"
notes: A fixed count is a safety cap, not a completion signal.
tool_use means Claude is waiting for results. Any other value ends or interrupts the loop.
Length says nothing about completion.
Text matching is fragile and easily wrong.

questions.stem: Claude's response contains two tool_use blocks. How should the application reply?
options: Two separate user messages, each with one tool_result
One user message with two ID-matched tool_result blocks
Only the first result; Claude will ask again for the second
One assistant message containing both of the results
notes: Results for one assistant turn belong in a single user message.
All results for a turn go back together, each linked to its request by ID.
Every tool_use needs a result or the request is invalid.
Tool results are sent in a user message.

questions.stem: A tool raises an exception inside an agent loop. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Let the exception end the process so that it is noticed
Return a tool_result with is_error true and a reason
Return a made-up success value to keep the flow simple
Return an empty string so that the loop carries on
notes: Crashing loses the task and the context.
The model can then retry, try another route, or explain the problem.
Fabricated results cause wrong answers.
Hiding the failure misleads the model.

questions.stem: An agent loop has a limit of 20 iterations. How should that limit be regarded?
options: As a target the agent should try to reach each time
As the normal way for the agent to finish its tasks
As a safety net that triggers escalation if reached
As unnecessary, since models always stop by themselves
notes: More turns are not better.
Finishing by exhaustion means the task did not complete properly.
Normal completion is signalled by stop_reason. A cap guards against runaway loops.
Loops can and do run away.

questions.stem: An agent calls the same search tool with the same query fifteen times in a row. The tool returns "Error" each time. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Raise the iteration limit so that the agent has more attempts
Remove the iteration limit to avoid cutting the agent off
Return a specific error and whether a retry can help
Raise the temperature so that the queries vary a little
notes: More attempts at the same failing call.
That removes the only protection.
With an informative error the model can change approach instead of repeating itself.
Random variation does not fix a failing tool.

questions.stem: An agent can issue refunds. Policy says refunds above a set amount must be approved by a manager, without exception. How should this be implemented?
options: A sentence in the system prompt stating the policy firmly
A lower temperature so that the agent follows the policy
A code check that blocks the tool until approved
A few-shot example showing the agent asking a manager
notes: Prompts guide behaviour but cannot guarantee it.
Sampling settings are not enforcement.
A rule that must always hold needs deterministic enforcement outside the model.
Examples make it likelier, not certain.

questions.stem: A team adds a human approval step before every tool call, including read-only lookups. Reviewers soon approve everything without reading. What is the better design?
options: Require two approvers for every single tool call
Remove approval entirely, since it isn't being read
Show reviewers less information so that they go faster
Require approval only for risky or irreversible actions
notes: That doubles the fatigue.
Risky actions would then be unguarded.
Reviewers need the exact action to judge it.
Gating by risk keeps reviews meaningful and avoids approval fatigue.

questions.stem: A lead agent delegates research to a sub-agent with the instruction "research the product we discussed". The sub-agent returns generic material. Why?
options: Sub-agents always ignore the first instruction given
Sub-agents cannot use search tools of any kind
Sub-agents are limited to the smallest model tier
Sub-agents start fresh and never saw that discussion
notes: There is no such behaviour.
They can be given tools.
They can use any configured model.
Everything a sub-agent needs must be passed explicitly in its task.

questions.stem: What is a main benefit of delegating a noisy exploration task to a sub-agent?
options: The sub-agent shares and extends the parent's context
The sub-agent's tokens are not billed to the account
The sub-agent's output is guaranteed to be correct
The noise stays out of the main context window
notes: It has a separate context.
All tokens are billed.
No such guarantee exists.
Context isolation keeps the lead agent's window focused.

questions.stem: A simple, strictly sequential task is split across five sub-agents. It becomes slower and more expensive, with no quality gain. What does this illustrate?
options: Multi-agent overhead only pays off for separable work
Five is too few; at least ten sub-agents are needed
Sub-agents should always be run on the largest tier
Sequential tasks cannot be done by language models
notes: Sub-agents pay off with parallel or specialised sub-tasks, not simple linear ones.
More agents add more overhead.
That would raise cost further.
A single agent or chain handles them well.

questions.stem: Using the Claude Agent SDK, a code-review agent must be able to read and search files but never modify them. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Set allowed_tools to read and search tools only
Set the temperature to 0 so that it stays cautious
Set max_turns to 1 so that there is no time to edit
Ask in the system prompt that files are not modified
notes: Restricting the tool set is least privilege, enforced by the SDK.
Temperature does not control tool access.
A turn limit does not remove the ability to edit.
A request, not a restriction.

questions.stem: When is the Claude Agent SDK a better choice than a hand-written loop on the Messages API?
options: When built-in tools, hooks and sessions are wanted
When the application makes one call with no tools
When token usage must go unrecorded
When no tool should ever run in the application
notes: The SDK packages the loop and the surrounding machinery.
A direct API call is simpler.
Neither approach hides usage.
The SDK's value is largely in tools.

questions.stem: A task requires a draft to be improved against clear quality criteria over several rounds. Which pattern fits?
options: A single call with a very high max_tokens value
Evaluator-optimiser: generate, critique, then revise
Parallelisation: produce ten drafts and return them all
Routing: classify the draft and send it to one handler
notes: More room does not add a review step.
Iterative refinement against criteria is exactly what this pattern provides.
That produces alternatives, not a refined result.
Routing selects a path; it does not iterate.

questions.stem: Which TWO are appropriate safety limits for an autonomous agent loop? (Select TWO.)
options: A maximum number of iterations
A total token or cost budget for the task
A minimum number of tool calls per turn
A temperature of exactly 1.0 on every call
A rule that the agent may never return end_turn
notes: Bounds how long a loop can run.
Bounds spending across all calls.
Forcing tool calls encourages needless work.
Temperature is not a safety limit.
That would stop it from finishing.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about returning tool results are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: tool_result blocks are placed in an assistant message
Each tool_result must reference the tool_use_id it answers
Results may be omitted for tools that returned nothing
A failed tool call should be returned with is_error set to true
Results must be summarised by a second model first
notes: They are sent in a user message.
The ID links a result to its request.
Every tool_use needs a result, even an empty one.
The model needs to know that it failed.
No such requirement exists.

questions.stem: A team wants long-running agents but does not want to build sandboxing, session storage and scaling. Data requirements permit a hosted service. Which option fits?
options: A nightly batch of unrelated summary requests
An Anthropic-hosted managed agent service
A hand-written loop on a developer's laptop
A single Messages API call with a long prompt
notes: Batches are not interactive agents.
A managed service runs the harness and infrastructure, which suits long-running and asynchronous work.
Not durable or scalable for long-running work.
One call is not a long-running agent.

questions.stem: An agent must read files on an internal network that cannot be exposed outside the company. Which deployment is most appropriate?
options: A hosted agent given the network's admin password
A self-hosted agent running inside the company network
A public MCP server that publishes the files
A chat app where staff paste the files by hand
notes: Sharing credentials outward defeats the restriction.
Self-hosting keeps the loop, files and credentials in the organisation's own environment.
Exposes what must stay private.
Manual, error-prone and not an agent.

questions.stem: A team needs an agent workflow with explicit steps, saved state between steps, and pauses for human approval. Which kind of framework is designed for this?
options: An object-relational mapper for the database
A unit-testing framework with assertion helpers
A graph-based framework such as LangGraph
A CSS framework for styling the approval screen
notes: Persistence libraries do not define agent control flow.
Testing tools do not orchestrate agents.
Graph frameworks model nodes, edges and state explicitly, with checkpoints and human-in-the-loop pauses.
Unrelated to agent orchestration.

questions.stem: What is the main risk of adopting an agent framework before understanding the underlying API calls?
options: Frameworks only work with the smallest model tier
Frameworks prevent the use of any tool definitions
The abstraction hides the prompts and requests
Frameworks make each API call cost twice as much
notes: They work with any tier.
Frameworks generally support tools.
When something goes wrong you need to see what was actually sent. Heavy abstraction can obscure it.
Pricing is unaffected by the framework itself.

questions.stem: When is a supervisor agent with several workers a good design?
options: When the task is a single short classification
When the token budget for the task is very limited
When the work splits into independent, parallel parts
When every step depends closely on the previous one
notes: Far too much machinery for one call.
Hierarchies multiply token use.
Hierarchies pay off for broad, separable work. For sequential tasks they add cost and hand-off errors.
Tightly coupled steps suit a single agent or a chain.

questions.stem: An agent keeps a single shared memory file for all users. One user's reply mentions another user's project. What design rule was broken?
options: Memory must be stored inside the system prompt
Memory must be written in upper-case letters only
Memory must be reloaded twice in each new session
Memory must be scoped per user or project
notes: Location in the prompt does not isolate users.
Formatting does not isolate users.
Reloading does not scope it.
Unscoped memory leaks information between users. Scope and load only what is relevant.

questions.stem: In an Agent SDK application, a rule must run every time before any shell command executes, whatever the model decides. Which feature provides this?
options: A lower limit on the number of turns
A sentence in the system prompt option
A description added to the sub-agent
A hook registered for the pre-tool-use event
notes: A turn cap does not inspect commands.
Advisory, not deterministic.
Descriptions guide delegation, not enforcement.
Hooks run deterministically at lifecycle points and can block the action.

questions.stem: What does a custom agent harness need to do that a single Messages API call does not?
options: Translate each prompt into a different language
Train the model on the user's documents first
Replace the system prompt after every single token
Run tools, feed results back, and decide when to stop
notes: Unrelated to what a harness does.
No training happens in a harness.
Not something a harness does.
A harness is the loop around the model: dispatching tools, managing context and enforcing limits.

questions.stem: A prompt says "Summarise this." The summaries vary widely in length and focus. What is the most effective first improvement?
options: State the audience, purpose, length and what to include
Set the max_tokens parameter to a very low value
Add "IMPORTANT" in capitals before the instruction
Switch to the largest model tier that is available
notes: Specific instructions and context are the first thing to fix.
That truncates rather than guides.
Emphasis without detail adds little.
The problem is an underspecified prompt.

questions.stem: A prompt includes three examples that are nearly identical. Outputs now copy their wording and structure too closely. What should change?
options: Use varied examples that cover different cases
Add ten more examples that are similar to those three
Move the three examples into the user's message
Remove every example and rely on the instructions
notes: Diverse examples show the pattern without anchoring on one instance.
Reinforces the over-fitting.
Location does not address their similarity.
Usually loses the format guidance examples provide.

questions.stem: A prompt places instructions and a pasted customer email in one block of text. Claude sometimes follows sentences from the email as if they were instructions. What structural change helps most?
options: Wrap the email in XML tags and refer to it by tag name
Put the email before the instructions without any markers
Write all of the instructions in capital letters
Shorten the email to its first two sentences
notes: Tags separate data from instructions clearly.
Order alone does not separate them.
Emphasis does not create a boundary.
Loses information and leaves the ambiguity.

questions.stem: A prompt contains a 60-page document and one question about it. Where should the question go for best results?
options: In the middle of the document, at a random page
After the document, at the end of the prompt
Before the document, at the very beginning only
In a separate request sent five minutes later
notes: The middle of long inputs gets the least attention.
With long inputs, placing the query last tends to improve answers.
Generally weaker than placing it after long content.
A separate request would not include the document.

questions.stem: A service needs every response to be valid JSON matching a fixed schema. Which approach gives the strongest guarantee?
options: One example of the JSON in the system prompt
Structured outputs with a JSON schema
An instruction: "Return only JSON, nothing else"
A regular expression that removes surrounding text
notes: Examples guide but do not guarantee.
Schema-constrained output guarantees the shape of the response.
Usually works but guarantees nothing.
Cleans up after the fact; invalid JSON can still occur.

questions.stem: A team uses structured outputs and removes all response checks, reasoning that the schema is guaranteed. Which case can still deliver an unusable response?
options: The model returns the properties in a different order
The output is cut off because max_tokens was reached
The model uses double quotes around the strings
The model inserts spaces between the JSON tokens
notes: Property order does not make JSON unusable.
Truncation and refusals fall outside the guarantee, so stop_reason must still be checked.
Double quotes are required by JSON.
Whitespace is valid JSON.

questions.stem: A response fails schema validation. Which retry strategy is most effective?
options: Raise the temperature and send the identical request
Accept the response and correct it by hand later
Send the error back and ask for a fix, with a limit
Send the identical request again until it validates
notes: More randomness reduces consistency.
Passes invalid data downstream.
Specific feedback lets the model fix the problem; a limit prevents endless loops.
A blind retry tends to repeat the error and may never end.

questions.stem: An extractor retries three times because the field "warranty_period" fails validation; the source document never mentions a warranty. What is the right fix?
options: Switch to a larger model to find the hidden value
Add an example with a typical warranty period
Allow null; retries cannot supply missing data
Increase the number of retries from three to ten
notes: There is no value to find.
Encourages the model to invent one.
When information is absent from the source, the schema must allow absence.
No number of retries creates missing data.

questions.stem: In a long support conversation the assistant starts quoting the wrong order number. Earlier turns were replaced by a summary to save tokens. What would prevent this?
options: Summarise more aggressively to free additional space
Raise the temperature so that the model re-reads context
Keep exact values in a facts block sent every turn
Ask the customer to repeat the number in each message
notes: Loses even more detail.
Temperature does not change what is in context.
Summaries blur precise details. Pinned facts keep them exact.
Poor experience and unnecessary.

questions.stem: An agent's context fills up with large results from file reads made many turns ago, which could be fetched again if needed. Which technique fits best?
options: Switch off tools so that no further results are added
Delete the system prompt to recover the most tokens
Duplicate the results so that they are not forgotten
Clear old tool results but keep the recent ones
notes: Stops the agent from working.
Removes the agent's instructions.
Uses even more context.
Stale, re-fetchable tool output is the cheapest thing to drop.

questions.stem: A question-answering feature over supplied documents sometimes states facts that are not in them. Which prompt technique reduces this most directly?
options: Tell the model that it is a world-class expert
Remove the documents and ask from memory instead
Raise the temperature to encourage a fuller answer
Ask for quotes first and allow "not found"
notes: A role does not ground answers in the documents.
Removes the grounding entirely.
More randomness tends to increase invention.
Grounding in quotes plus permission to say the answer is absent reduces invention.

questions.stem: A response from a structured-output request must be checked before use. Which TWO checks remain necessary? (Select TWO.)
options: That stop_reason does not indicate truncation or refusal
That the response is longer than the prompt
